# JSON Schema

> Convert Types to JSON Schema and back, and compare schemas in any format

# Overview

> Generate JSON Schema from a Type, read a JSON Schema or a Zod schema into a Type, and compare schemas from any of them.

ArkType converts in both directions, and once a schema is a Type, it compares with any other.

| direction | API |
| - | - |
| Type → JSON Schema | `T.toJsonSchema()`, `T["~standard"].jsonSchema` |
| JSON Schema or Standard Schema → Type | `fromJsonSchema(schema)` |
| compare any of them | `.extends()`, `.equals()`, `.overlaps()` |

## Type to JSON Schema

Every Type has a `toJsonSchema()` method. Nothing else to install:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

const schema = User.toJsonSchema()
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"name": { "type": "string" },
		"age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }
	},
	"required": ["name"]
}
```

Some things a Type can check, like a `Date`, a `bigint` or a custom `narrow`, have no JSON Schema equivalent. `toJsonSchema()` throws on those unless you tell it what to write instead. See [To JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema).

Libraries that accept any [Standard JSON Schema](https://standardschema.dev/json-schema) read it from `T["~standard"].jsonSchema`, which never throws for those parts. See [Standard JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#standard-json-schema).

## JSON Schema to Type

`fromJsonSchema` reads a JSON Schema into a Type:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const User = fromJsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: {
		name: { type: "string" },
		age: { type: "integer", minimum: 0 }
	},
	required: ["name"]
})

User.expression // "{ name: string, age?: number % 1 >= 0 } & isNonArray"
// ArkErrors: age must be an integer
User({ name: "Ada", age: 1.5 })
```

A schema written in the call infers its type, so `User` is a `Type<{ name: string; age?: number }>`. It reads a [Standard JSON Schema](https://standardschema.dev/json-schema), like a Zod schema, too. See [From JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema), and [Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) for which keywords it understands.

Schemas are code-equivalent: `fromJsonSchema` prevents code injection and prototype pollution, but does not guard against catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) in user-supplied `pattern` or `patternProperties` regexes or combinatorial `allOf` blow-up.

## Compare schemas

Read into Types, JSON Schemas, Zod schemas and your own Types compare with each other, so you can check in CI that a new version of an API schema still accepts everything the old one did:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"
import { z } from "zod"

const V1 = fromJsonSchema(z.object({ id: z.string(), age: z.number() }))
const V2 = fromJsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: { id: { type: "string" }, age: { type: "number" } },
	required: ["id"]
})

V1.extends(V2) // true: V2 accepts everything V1 did
V2.extends(V1) // false: V2 accepts { id: "a" }
```

[Compare schemas](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/compare) covers every comparison and what `true` proves.

# To JSON Schema

> Generate a JSON Schema from any Type, pick a draft, and decide what to write for what JSON Schema can't express.

Every Type has a `toJsonSchema()` method:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

const schema = User.toJsonSchema()
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"name": { "type": "string" },
		"age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }
	},
	"required": ["name"]
}
```

A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) validator has `toJsonSchema()`, its schema baked at build time, where its build sees code call it or its [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) option sets it.

## Options

| option | default | effect |
| - | - | - |
| `target` | `"draft-2020-12"` | what to write, `"draft-2020-12"`, `"draft-07"`, [`"openapi-3.0"`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#openapi-30) or [`"openapi-3.1"`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#openapi-31) |
| `dialect` | the target's URL | the `$schema` value. `null` omits it. Takes precedence over `target`'s URL |
| `useRefs` | `false` | write every part once under `$defs`, not only [cyclic aliases](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#cyclic-types), and point to it with `$ref` |
| `aliasDefs` | `false` | write [a scope's aliases](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#named-aliases) once under `$defs`, named by the alias, not only cyclic ones |
| `discriminator` | `true` for `"openapi-3.0"` / `"openapi-3.1"` | name the key a [discriminated union](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#discriminated-unions)'s `oneOf` is told apart by with OpenAPI's `discriminator` |
| `io` | unset | convert `"in"` (input) or `"out"` (output) instead of the Type as written. See [`io`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#io) |
| `fallback` | throws | what to write for a part JSON Schema can't express. See [Fallbacks](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallbacks) |

### target

The drafts differ in how they write tuples and where they put definitions:

```ts
const Pair = type(["string", "number"])

Pair.toJsonSchema()
// {
// 	$schema: "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
// 	type: "array",
// 	minItems: 2,
// 	prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }],
// 	items: false
// }

Pair.toJsonSchema({ target: "draft-07" })
// {
// 	$schema: "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
// 	type: "array",
// 	minItems: 2,
// 	items: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }],
// 	additionalItems: false
// }
```

`draft-07` writes `definitions` where `draft-2020-12` writes `$defs`.

### OpenAPI 3.0

`"openapi-3.0"` writes an [OpenAPI 3.0 Schema Object](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.0.3#schema-object), which has no `$schema` and words some keywords differently:

| draft 2020-12 | `"openapi-3.0"` |
| - | - |
| `exclusiveMinimum: 0` | `minimum: 0`, `exclusiveMinimum: true` |
| `type: "string"`, `const: "cat"` | `type: "string"`, `enum: ["cat"]` |
| `not: { const: 5 }` | `not: { enum: [5] }` |
| `anyOf: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "null" }]` | `type: "string"`, `nullable: true` |
| `type: "null"` | `type: "string"`, `nullable: true`, `enum: [null]` |
| `examples: ["a", "b"]` | `example: "a"` |
| `contentEncoding: "base64"` | `format: "byte"` |
| `contentMediaType: "application/json"` | left out |
| `type: "array"` | `type: "array"`, `items: {}` |

`nullable` adds `null` only to the `type` beside it, and an `enum` there must list `null` too. A union whose other branches share no `type`, like `string | number | null`, keeps `null` as a branch of its `anyOf`. OpenAPI 3.0 has no `null` type, so `null` alone is written as zod writes it: a `nullable` string whose `enum` allows only `null`.

What OpenAPI 3.0 can't express goes to a [fallback](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallbacks), so `toJsonSchema()` throws for it by default:

- A tuple's elements, since `items` is one schema for every element, go to `arrayPrefix`.
- `patternProperties` and `propertyNames` go to `indexKey`. A `string` index signature is still `additionalProperties`, unless a declared key's value allows more than its own.
- Definitions go to `defs`. A `$ref` points into the document's `#/components/schemas`, which a Schema Object can't hold, so the handler receives them to put there:

```ts
import { scope, type JsonSchema } from "arktype"

const types = scope({ Node: { value: "number", "next?": "Node" } }).export()

const components: Record<string, JsonSchema> = {}

// { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Node" }
const schema = types.Node.toJsonSchema({
	target: "openapi-3.0",
	fallback: {
		defs: ctx => {
			// { Node: { type: "object", properties: { ... } } }
			Object.assign(components, ctx.defs)
			return ctx.base
		}
	}
})
```

zod, valibot and sury write a tuple as an array whose elements may each be any of its elements, which accepts `[1, "a"]` for `["string", "number"]`. To write it that way:

```ts
const Pair = type(["string", "number"])

// {
// 	type: "array",
// 	items: { anyOf: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }] },
// 	minItems: 2,
// 	maxItems: 2
// }
Pair.toJsonSchema({
	target: "openapi-3.0",
	fallback: {
		arrayPrefix: ({ base, elements, items }) => ({
			...base,
			items: { anyOf: items ? [...elements, items] : elements }
		})
	}
})
```

OpenAPI 3.0 names a media type where a request's body is, not in a schema, so `string.json` is a `string` with no `contentMediaType`. [`jsonSchema` meta](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#your-own-schema) you configure is written as configured, `contentMediaType` included.

### OpenAPI 3.1

`"openapi-3.1"` writes an [OpenAPI 3.1 Schema Object](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.1#schema-object), which is `draft-2020-12` without `$schema`, but for its `$ref`s: like OpenAPI 3.0's, they point into `#/components/schemas`, and the definitions go to [`defs`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#openapi-30) for you to put there.

Standard JSON Schema has no `"openapi-3.1"` target, so `~standard.jsonSchema` doesn't take it, and a [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) validator writes it only where it's [configured](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#configuration).

### dialect

```ts
type("string").toJsonSchema({ dialect: null }) // { type: "string" }
```

### io

`io` chooses which side of a morph, defaulted key, `"+": "delete"` object or `undefined`-allowing property to convert:

- **unset** (default): converts the Type's input while keeping output-side structure except `"+": "delete"` (so morphs hit the `morph` fallback, defaults stay `default`, and `"+": "delete"` omits `additionalProperties`).
- **`"in"`**: converts the input (morphs as their input, keeps `default`, drops `undefined` union branches, and allows keys `"+": "delete"` removes).
- **`"out"`**: converts the output (morphs as their output, applies defaults, writes `additionalProperties: false` for `"+": "delete"`, and drops `undefined` from object property/index values while omitting `undefined`-allowing object properties from `required`); paired with a base fallback (`fallback: ctx => ctx.base`), it matches [`~standard.jsonSchema.output`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#standard-json-schema).

### Cyclic types

A cyclic alias is written once under `$defs`, named by its alias, and each reference to it is a `$ref`. Everything else, including an alias that isn't cyclic, is written inline:

```ts
const types = scope({ Node: { value: "number", "next?": "Node" } }).export()

const schema = types.Node.toJsonSchema()
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"$ref": "#/$defs/Node",
	"$defs": {
		"Node": {
			"type": "object",
			"properties": {
				"value": { "type": "number" },
				"next": { "$ref": "#/$defs/Node" }
			},
			"required": ["value"]
		}
	}
}
```

- A generic's instantiations are named by the generic, like `Box` for `Box<string>`, and a submodule's alias by its own name, like `B` for `A.B`.
- A name another definition already has is numbered from 2, like `Node2`, in the order the definitions are reached.
- A cycle with no alias, like a `this` reference, is named by what ArkType calls it, like `type`.
- `.in`, `.out` and `~standard.jsonSchema` name definitions the same way.

### Named aliases

`aliasDefs: true` writes every alias of a scope under `$defs`, like a cyclic one, so an OpenAPI document's components keep their names:

```ts
const types = scope({
	Address: { street: "string" },
	User: { home: "Address", "work?": "Address | null" }
}).export()

const schema = types.User.toJsonSchema({ aliasDefs: true })
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"$ref": "#/$defs/User",
	"$defs": {
		"User": {
			"type": "object",
			"properties": {
				"home": { "$ref": "#/$defs/Address" },
				"work": { "anyOf": [{ "$ref": "#/$defs/Address" }, { "type": "null" }] }
			},
			"required": ["home"]
		},
		"Address": {
			"type": "object",
			"properties": { "street": { "type": "string" } },
			"required": ["street"]
		}
	}
}
```

- An alias of a basis, like `Id: "string"`, is written inline, since every `string` would be a `$ref` to it. So is a private alias.
- A list of names, like `aliasDefs: ["Address", "#Secret"]`, writes exactly those, private and basis ones included. A name no scope it reaches has throws.
- A Type of the scope used in another, like `type({ to: types.Address })`, is still named.
- A submodule's alias is named by its own name, like `Zip` for `Geo.Zip`, and its root by the submodule's.
- What's named is a part equal to the alias's resolution, wherever it is: a non-cyclic alias leaves no trace in what references it. Of two aliases with the same resolution, the first is the name of both, and an alias given other meta where it's used, like `Address.describe("home")`, is a new part and is inlined.
- Set it [on a scope](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#configuration) to write that scope's Types this way by default. For `openapi-3.0` and `openapi-3.1`, the definitions go to [`defs`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#openapi-30), so calling `toJsonSchema` for each of a module's Types collects every component.

## How Types map

| ArkType | JSON Schema |
| - | - |
| `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"null"` | `type` |
| `"number.integer"`, `"number % 2"` | `type: "integer"`, plus `multipleOf: 2` |
| `"0 < number <= 1"` | `exclusiveMinimum: 0`, `maximum: 1` |
| `"string >= 1"`, `"string == 2"` | `minLength`, or `minLength` and `maxLength` |
| `"string[] > 0"` | `items`, `minItems: 1` |
| `["string", "number?"]` | `prefixItems`, `minItems: 1`, `items: false` |
| `/^a/` | `pattern: "^a"` |
| `"string.email"`, `"string.uuid"` | `pattern`, `format: "email"`, `"uuid"` |
| `"string.ip.v4"`, `"string.ip.v6"` | `pattern`, `format: "ipv4"`, `"ipv6"` |
| `"string.date.iso"` | `pattern`, `format: "date-time"` |
| `"string.base64"` | `pattern`, `contentEncoding: "base64"` |
| `"string.base64.url"` | `pattern`, `contentEncoding: "base64url"` |
| `"string.date"`, `"string.url"`, `"string.regex"` | `format: "date-time"`, `"uri"`, `"regex"` |
| `"string.json"` | `contentMediaType: "application/json"` |
| `"'a' \| 'b'"` | `type: "string"`, `enum: ["a", "b"]` |
| `"string \| null"` | `anyOf` |
| `{ kind: "'a'", a: "string" }` or `{ kind: "'b'" }` | [`oneOf`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#discriminated-unions) |
| `{ "name?": "string" }` | `properties`, with only required keys in `required` |
| `{ "+": "reject", ... }` | `additionalProperties: false` |
| `"Record<string, number>"` | `additionalProperties: {...}` |
| `{ id: "string", "[string]": "string" }` | `additionalProperties: {...}` |
| `{ id: "string \| number", "[string]": "string" }` | `patternProperties: { "": {...} }` |
| `{ "[/^x-/]": "string" }` | `patternProperties: { "^x-": {...} }` |
| `{ "[string <= 3]": "number", "+": "reject" }` | `propertyNames`, `additionalProperties: {...}` |
| `{ role: "string = 'user'" }` | `default: "user"` on `role` |
| `.describe("...")`, `.configure({ title, examples })` | `description`, `title`, `examples` |

JSON Schema's `pattern` has no flags, and validators like Ajv read every pattern with `u`. `d` and `g` don't change what a regex matches, so they're left out, as is `u` for draft 2020-12 and OpenAPI 3.1, whose patterns are read with it. Any other flag, like `i` in `/^a/i`, goes to the [`patternFlags`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) fallback, as does a regex without `u` that fails or parses differently under `u`, like `/^a\-b$/` or `/^\p{L}$/`, with `flags: ""`.

An index signature applies to every key, including declared ones. JSON Schema skips declared keys in `additionalProperties`, so a `string` index signature is written there only if each declared key's value is already within the index's, as `id` is above. Otherwise it's written as `patternProperties` with a pattern every key matches, which checks the declared keys too. OpenAPI 3.0 and some LLM structured output APIs have no `patternProperties`, so they can read only the first.

A keyword's `pattern` has no lookaround or backreference, so a validator reading patterns with RE2, as some LLMs' structured outputs do, reads it as arktype's regex does. Your own regex is written as you wrote it, unless it fails or parses differently under `u`, as above.

A keyword's `format`, `contentEncoding` or `contentMediaType` names what its strings are. JSON Schema reads each as an annotation, which a validator doesn't check unless it's configured to, so it's written whether or not arktype's check matches the standard's definition exactly. A keyword checked by a regex is written with that `pattern` too, so a validator that ignores formats still checks what arktype does. One checked by a function is written as its format alone: `string.date` accepts whatever `Date` parses, and `string.url` whatever `URL.canParse` does, so their schemas accept strings the Type rejects. A validator that asserts formats, like Ajv with `ajv-formats`, can also reject strings arktype accepts, where a format's RFC differs from arktype's check: `date-time` requires a time that `string.date` and `string.date.iso` don't, and `uri` rejects the space in a path that `string.url` accepts. Keywords no format names, like `string.date.epoch` or `string.creditCard`, go to the [`predicate`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) fallback.

A key that isn't `string` or a single regex, like `[string <= 3]`, needs `propertyNames`, which checks every key of the object. That's only the same thing when every key must match it: undeclared keys are rejected, it's the only index signature, and every declared key matches it. Its value is then `additionalProperties`, or, if a declared key's value allows more than it does, `patternProperties: { "": {...} }`. Any other such key goes to the [`indexKey`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) fallback.

### Discriminated unions

A union whose object branches each require a string at one key, no value of which two branches allow, is written as `oneOf`, since no data can match two of its branches. For `"openapi-3.0"` and `"openapi-3.1"`, or where the `discriminator` option is `true`, it names that key with OpenAPI's [`discriminator`](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.0.3#discriminator-object), so a code generator models it as a tagged union:

```ts
const Destination = type({ type: "'bankAccount'", routing: "string" }).or({
	type: "'card'",
	last4: "string"
})

const schema = Destination.toJsonSchema({ target: "openapi-3.0" })
```

```json
{
	"oneOf": [
		{
			"type": "object",
			"properties": {
				"last4": { "type": "string" },
				"type": { "type": "string", "enum": ["card"] }
			},
			"required": ["last4", "type"]
		},
		{
			"type": "object",
			"properties": {
				"routing": { "type": "string" },
				"type": { "type": "string", "enum": ["bankAccount"] }
			},
			"required": ["routing", "type"]
		}
	],
	"discriminator": { "propertyName": "type" }
}
```

- The key is the first one the first branch requires that tells every branch apart.
- A branch that's a `$ref`, like a [cyclic alias](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#cyclic-types) or any part with `useRefs`, is listed in `discriminator.mapping` under each value it allows. An inline branch is found by its own value.
- `discriminator` isn't a JSON Schema keyword, and Ajv rejects it unless its `discriminator` option is set, so draft targets write it only where the option is `true`, as an OpenAPI 3.1 document reads it.
- Any other union is `anyOf`: one where two branches allow the same value, a branch doesn't require the key, the values aren't strings, or a branch isn't an object. A `null` branch is written beside the `oneOf`: `anyOf: [{ oneOf: [...] }, { type: "null" }]`.

### never

`never`, which accepts nothing, is `{ not: {} }` for every target. An empty `enum` would say the same, but OpenAPI 3.0 requires an `enum` to list something, and LLM APIs like OpenAI's reject it. An optional key of `undefined` alone, like `{ "b?": "undefined" }`, is `never` in JSON, which can only leave it out.

## Your own schema

Configure `jsonSchema` meta to write a Type's schema yourself. It replaces the schema the Type's constraints imply, so a `narrow` it covers needs no fallback:

```ts
const Even = type("number")
	.narrow(n => n % 2 === 0)
	.configure({ jsonSchema: { type: "integer", multipleOf: 2 } })

Even.toJsonSchema() // { $schema: "...", type: "integer", multipleOf: 2 }
```

The Type's other meta, like a description, is still written beside it. Unlike other meta, `jsonSchema` is configured on the Type alone, not on the Types it references, since it describes the whole Type.

### Meta

Meta is written only where it's a JSON Schema annotation: `title`, `description`, `default`, `examples`, `deprecated`, `readOnly`, `writeOnly`, `$comment`, `format`, `contentEncoding` and `contentMediaType`, plus any key starting with `x-` you add to [`ArkEnv.meta`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#metadata). Anything else, like `alias`, `onFail`, the words configured for errors or another key you add, is left out, since strict validators like Ajv's, OpenAPI 3.0 and LLM APIs reject keywords they don't know. To write another key, put it in `jsonSchema`:

```ts
const Id = type("string").configure({
	alias: "Id", // left out
	readOnly: true,
	jsonSchema: { type: "string", $id: "https://example.com/id" }
})

Id.toJsonSchema() // { $schema: "...", readOnly: true, type: "string", $id: "https://example.com/id" }
```

OpenAPI 3.0 has no `$comment` or `contentMediaType`, so they're left out of its schemas.

## Fallbacks

Some things a Type checks have no JSON Schema equivalent: a `Date`, a `bigint`, a morph, a `narrow`. By default, `toJsonSchema()` throws a `ToJsonSchemaError` for them, naming where it is and which fallback to configure:

```ts
type({ at: "Date" }).toJsonSchema() // throws ToJsonSchemaError (code "date")
```

Pass a handler for its [code](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) to write something instead. The handler receives the schema written so far as `ctx.base`, plus fields for its code, and returns the schema to use:

```ts
const Event = type({ name: "string", at: "Date" })

const schema = Event.toJsonSchema({
	fallback: {
		date: ctx => ({ ...ctx.base, type: "string", format: "date-time" })
	}
})
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"at": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" },
		"name": { "type": "string" }
	},
	"required": ["at", "name"]
}
```

A `default` handler covers every code you don't list. Passing a function instead of an object is the same as passing it as `default`. Return `ctx.base` to leave out what JSON Schema can't express:

```ts
// properties.at is now {}
Event.toJsonSchema({ fallback: ctx => ctx.base })
```

Leaving something out makes the schema accept values the Type rejects.

A default is a value, not a schema, so `defaultValue` has no `base`, and `ctx => ctx.base` leaves the default out. Its handler returns the JSON to write as the default, or `undefined` to omit it.

### Morphs

A morph has a different input and output, so there is no single schema for it. Convert one side with `.in` or `.out`:

```ts
const Tags = type("string")
	.pipe(s => s.split(","))
	.to("string[]")

Tags.in.toJsonSchema() // { $schema: "...", type: "string" }
Tags.out.toJsonSchema() // { $schema: "...", type: "array", items: { type: "string" } }
```

### annotatingFallback

To keep what JSON Schema can't express rather than drop it, pass `annotatingFallback`. It writes each such constraint as an `x-arktype-*` keyword, naming a function, class or symbol by its `$ark` name as a Type's `.json` does:

```ts
import { annotatingFallback, type } from "arktype"

const schema = type({
	id: "bigint",
	createdAt: "Date"
}).toJsonSchema({ fallback: annotatingFallback })
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"createdAt": { "x-arktype-proto": "Date" },
		"id": { "x-arktype-domain": "bigint" }
	},
	"required": ["createdAt", "id"]
}
```

Validators ignore those keywords, so the schema still accepts values the Type rejects.

### Fallback codes

Every reason `toJsonSchema()` can throw, with the fields its handler receives besides `code` and `base`:

| code | raised for | example | fields |
| - | - | - | - |
| `arrayObject` | an array with named properties | `type("string[]").and({ n: "number" })` | `object` |
| `arrayPostfix` | elements after a variadic element | `type(["...", "string[]", "number"])` | `elements` |
| `arrayPrefix` | for `openapi-3.0`, elements before any variadic element | `type(["string", "number"])` | `elements`, and `items` for the rest, if any |
| `date` | a `Date`, once with all its bounds | `type("Date")` | `before`, `after`, `notEqual` (a list) |
| `defaultValue` | a default that isn't JSON. Return `undefined` to omit it | `type({ n: "bigint = 5n" })`, after `domain` | `value` |
| `defs` | for OpenAPI, the definitions `$ref`s point to | a cyclic Type | `defs`, by name |
| `domain` | `bigint` or `symbol` | `type("bigint")` | `domain` |
| `indexKey` | a key `propertyNames` can't express, or `additionalProperties` can't in `openapi-3.0` | `type({ "[string <= 3]": "number" })` | `key` and `value`, as schemas |
| `morph` | a morph | `type("string.trim")` | `out`, the output schema or `null` |
| `patternFlags` | a regex flag other than `d`, `g` or, for 2020-12 and 3.1, `u`, or a flagless regex incompatible with `u` | `type(/^a/i)` | `pattern`, `flags` |
| `patternIntersection` | a second regex on the same string | `type(/^a/).and(/b$/)` | `pattern` |
| `predicate` | a `narrow` | `type("number").narrow(n => n > 0)` | `predicate` |
| `proto` | an `instanceof` other than `Array` or `Date` | `type("Map")` | `proto` |
| `symbolKey` | a symbol key or index signature | `type({ "[symbol]": "string" })` | `key` (`null` for an index), `value`, `optional` |
| `unit` | a literal that isn't JSON | `type("undefined")` | `unit` |

A `Date` is reported as `date`, never `proto`.

`object.json` accepts only arrays and objects whose prototype is `Object.prototype` or `null`. JSON Schema can't require that, but parsed JSON has no other kind of object, so it's written as any object or array:

```ts
// { $schema: "...", anyOf: [{ type: "object" }, { type: "array", items: {} }] }
type("object.json").toJsonSchema()
```

## Configuration

`toJsonSchema` options can also be set [globally or on a scope](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#levels). Options passed to `toJsonSchema()` are merged over them:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({
	toJsonSchema: {
		target: "draft-07",
		fallback: {
			date: ctx => ({ ...ctx.base, type: "string", format: "date-time" })
		}
	}
})
```

```ts
// import your config file before arktype
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// $schema is draft-07's, and at is { type: "string", format: "date-time" }
type({ at: "Date" }).toJsonSchema()
```

A handler passed to `toJsonSchema()` replaces the configured one for its code. A `default` passed there replaces every configured handler.

## Standard JSON Schema

Libraries that accept any [Standard JSON Schema](https://standardschema.dev/json-schema) read a Type's schema from `~standard.jsonSchema`. `input` describes what the Type accepts, `output` what it returns after its morphs:

```ts
const Form = type({
	tags: type("string")
		.pipe(s => s.split(","))
		.to("string[]"),
	"id?": "bigint"
})

// properties: { tags: { type: "string" }, id: {} }
Form["~standard"].jsonSchema.input({ target: "draft-2020-12" })

// properties: { tags: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } }, id: {} }
Form["~standard"].jsonSchema.output({ target: "draft-2020-12" })
```

Unlike `toJsonSchema()`, these never throw for a part JSON Schema can't express. They write as much of it as JSON Schema can describe, or `{}` if nothing, so `id` above accepts any value. A regex `patternFlags` covers is left out too, and so is an index signature `propertyNames` can't express, along with the `additionalProperties: false` that would reject the keys it allows.

- `target` must be `"draft-2020-12"`, `"draft-07"` or `"openapi-3.0"`. Anything else throws.
- For `"openapi-3.0"`, a tuple is an array of its length. A Schema Object has nowhere to put definitions, so they're written as `definitions` beside the schema, and each `$ref` points there, like `#/definitions/Node`, as zod writes them. The schema resolves its own `$ref`s as returned. To put it in an OpenAPI document, move `definitions` to `components.schemas` and replace `#/definitions/` with `#/components/schemas/` in its `$ref`s. A `defs` handler you configure gets `#/components/schemas/` `$ref`s, as `toJsonSchema()`'s does.
- `libraryOptions` are passed to `toJsonSchema()` as options, e.g. `{ dialect: null }`.
- Fallback handlers you configure or pass in `libraryOptions` still apply. Only the default throwing handlers are replaced.
- A second regex on a string is kept in `allOf`, as `annotatingFallback` writes it.
- `input` writes each morph's input, so it never calls a `morph` handler. It keeps defaults, and allows keys `"+": "delete"` would remove.

# From JSON Schema

> Read a JSON Schema, or a Standard JSON Schema like a Zod schema, into a Type with fromJsonSchema, and infer its type.

`fromJsonSchema` reads a JSON Schema into a Type:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const User = fromJsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: {
		name: { type: "string" },
		age: { type: "integer", minimum: 0 }
	},
	required: ["name"]
})

User.expression // "{ name: string, age?: number % 1 >= 0 } & isNonArray"
User({ name: "Ada" }) // { name: "Ada" }
// ArkErrors: age must be an integer
User({ name: "Ada", age: 1.5 })
```

`true` reads as `unknown` and `false` as `never`. The result is a Type like any other, so it validates, composes into definitions and [compares](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/compare) with Types, other JSON Schemas and schemas from other libraries.

## What it reads

`fromJsonSchema` takes one of:

- a **JSON Schema**: an object or a boolean, read as [Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) describes.
- a **[Standard JSON Schema](https://standardschema.dev/json-schema)**: a schema whose `~standard` has `jsonSchema`, like one from Zod 4.2.0 or later, read as the draft 2020-12 JSON Schema of its input, so what that can't express, like Zod's refinements, transforms and `undefined`, is left out. An arktype Type is read as its own input directly, keeping non-JSON domains like `Date` and narrows; pass `T.toJsonSchema()` to read it by JSON Schema's rules. Pass any other library's schema as its JSON Schema, like `z.toJSONSchema(schema)` before Zod 4.2.0.

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"
import { z } from "zod"

const User = fromJsonSchema(z.object({ name: z.string(), age: z.number() }))

User.expression // "{ age: number, name: string } & isNonArray"
```

Anything else throws a `ParseError`, as does a Standard Schema without `~standard.jsonSchema`, which is also a type error, and one whose `~standard.jsonSchema` throws, like Zod's for `z.date()`, with the library's error as its `cause`.

An object meant as neither, like the definition `{ name: "string" }`, reads today as a JSON Schema whose keywords are all unknown, which accepts everything, so `fromJsonSchema({ name: "string" })` is `unknown`; what such an object means is unspecified, and a minor release may throw for it.

## Inferring its type

`fromJsonSchema` infers the type of a JSON Schema written in the call, or declared `as const`:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const User = fromJsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: {
		name: { type: "string" },
		tags: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } }
	},
	required: ["name"]
})

// { name: string; tags?: string[] }
type User = typeof User.infer
```

The inferred type never rejects a value the schema accepts, but it can be wider: constraints like `minimum` and `pattern` don't narrow it, and a `$ref` that isn't a JSON Pointer, like one to an anchor, infers `unknown`. Inference follows `$ref`s into `$defs`, `definitions` and OpenAPI `components.schemas`, including recursive ones, and composition, `if`/`then`/`else` and `not`.

A Standard Schema infers its input, as `StandardSchemaV1.InferInput` does. A JSON Schema TypeScript can't see as a literal, like one parsed from a `.json` file, infers `unknown`. If you know its shape, annotate the result:

```ts
const User: Type<{ name: string }> = fromJsonSchema(userJson) as never

// { name: string }
const user = User.assert({ name: "Ada" })
```

The annotation isn't checked against the schema, so keep the two in sync yourself.

## How it reads JSON Schema

A Type read from a JSON Schema accepts exactly what a JSON Schema 2020-12 validator accepts, except that lengths count UTF-16 code units, with ajv as the tiebreaker. Every keyword in a schema applies, local `$ref`s resolve, including recursive ones, and draft-07 forms like `items` arrays and `definitions` are read too:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const Tree = fromJsonSchema({
	$defs: {
		Node: {
			type: "object",
			properties: {
				value: { type: "number" },
				children: { type: "array", items: { $ref: "#/$defs/Node" } }
			},
			required: ["value"]
		}
	},
	$ref: "#/$defs/Node"
})

Tree.allows({ value: 1, children: [{ value: 2 }] }) // true
```

A `$ref` resolves against the schema it's in, so to read a schema from an OpenAPI document, spread the document into a schema that refers to it:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const openApi = {
	openapi: "3.1.0",
	components: {
		schemas: {
			User: {
				type: "object",
				properties: { name: { type: "string" } },
				required: ["name"]
			}
		}
	}
} as const

const User = fromJsonSchema({ ...openApi, $ref: "#/components/schemas/User" })

User.allows({ name: "Ada" }) // true
```

OpenAPI 3.0's `nullable: true` adds `null` to the `type` beside it, as ajv reads it, and infers it there too. A `nullable` without a `type`, like one beside a `$ref`, throws a `ParseError`, as ajv does.

A schema's `description` is kept on `T.description` and metadata so it round-trips through `toJsonSchema()`, without replacing validation error `expected` phrasing.

[Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) lists how each keyword is read. `fromJsonSchema` prevents code injection and prototype pollution, so a schema can't run arbitrary code, but it compiles `pattern` and `patternProperties` with JavaScript's `RegExp` and intersects `allOf` branches eagerly: don't pass untrusted regexes that can backtrack catastrophically or deeply nested `allOf` combinations without bounding the input.

## Invalid schemas

A JSON Schema written in the call is checked as you write it:

```ts
// TypeScript: minLength must be a non-negative integer (was -1)
fromJsonSchema({ type: "string", minLength: -1 })

// TypeScript: unevaluatedProperties isn't supported by fromJsonSchema
fromJsonSchema({ type: "object", unevaluatedProperties: false })
```

`fromJsonSchema` throws a `ParseError` naming the keyword's JSON Pointer for an invalid keyword TypeScript can't check, like a `pattern`, or one it can't read exactly, like a `$ref` to another document:

```ts
// ParseError: #/pattern must be a valid pattern (was "[")
fromJsonSchema({ type: "string", pattern: "[" })

// ParseError: #/$ref must reference a schema in its own document (was https://example.com/user.json)
fromJsonSchema({ $ref: "https://example.com/user.json" })
```

Of the keywords it can't read, `$dynamicRef`, `$recursiveRef`, `unevaluatedItems`, `unevaluatedProperties` and a draft-04 boolean `exclusiveMinimum` or `exclusiveMaximum` are type errors too.

One check is deliberately stricter than JSON Schema: a `required` key a schema's own `properties` don't declare is a type error where nothing else could declare it. That's a schema with no `patternProperties`, composition keyword, `$ref` or dependent schema, whose `additionalProperties` is absent or `false`, reached from the root only through the `properties`, `additionalProperties`, `items` or `prefixItems` of schemas like it. JSON Schema reads the key as required with any value, but it's usually a typo.

## Typing a schema

To check a schema you declare separately without reading it, use `JsonSchema` from `arktype`:

```ts
import type { JsonSchema } from "arktype"

const Age = {
	type: "integer",
	minimum: 0
} satisfies JsonSchema.Numeric
```

## Back to JSON Schema

A Type from `fromJsonSchema` has [`toJsonSchema()`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema) like any other, so reading a schema and writing it back normalizes it. Keywords [Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) lists as opaque, like `uniqueItems`, `not` and `if`, come back as [`predicate` fallbacks](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes), so `toJsonSchema()` throws for them unless you handle that code.

# Compare schemas

> Check whether JSON Schemas, Zod schemas and Types accept the same values, a subset of each other's or none in common, and combine them.

Every Type knows the set of values it accepts, and [`fromJsonSchema`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema) reads a JSON Schema or a Standard JSON Schema, like a Zod schema, into a Type. Together, they compare schemas in any of those formats with each other and with your own Types:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"
import { z } from "zod"

const V1 = fromJsonSchema(
	z.object({ id: z.string(), age: z.number().int().min(0) })
)

const V2 = fromJsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: { id: { type: "string" }, age: { type: "number" } },
	required: ["id"]
})

// V2 is backwards compatible: it accepts everything V1 did
V1.extends(V2) // true
// but not the other way around: V2 accepts { id: "a" }
V2.extends(V1) // false
```

Use it to check in CI that a new version of an API schema still accepts what the old one did, to find out whether two schemas can ever accept the same value, to merge schemas from different libraries into one, or to normalize any of them to JSON Schema.

## Comparisons

| method | `true` means |
| - | - |
| `l.extends(r)` | every value `l` accepts, `r` accepts |
| `l.equals(r)` | `l` and `r` accept exactly the same values |
| `l.overlaps(r)` | some value is accepted by both |

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"
import { z } from "zod"

fromJsonSchema({ type: "integer", minimum: 0 }).equals(
	type("number.integer >= 0")
) // true

fromJsonSchema({ enum: ["a", "b"] }).extends(
	fromJsonSchema({ type: "string", maxLength: 1 })
) // true

fromJsonSchema({ type: "string", maxLength: 2 }).overlaps(
	fromJsonSchema(z.string().min(3))
) // false
```

Each method takes a definition, so pass a JSON Schema through `fromJsonSchema` first: `.or({ type: "number" })` is an object with a `type` key.

## What `true` proves

A comparison is sound for what each schema is read as: `true` is a proof. A Type is read exactly and a JSON Schema as [Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) describes.

`false` from `.extends()` or `.equals()` means the relation couldn't be proven, either because it doesn't hold or because a schema checks something the algebra can't reason about. Those are the JSON Schema keywords [Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) lists as opaque, like `not`, `uniqueItems` and `if`, and a Type's [`narrow`](https://arktype.io/docs/expressions#narrow) predicates:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

// true, but not provable through `not`
fromJsonSchema({ type: "string" }).extends(
	fromJsonSchema({ not: { type: "number" } })
) // false
```

An opaque keyword is still compared with itself, so a schema with `uniqueItems: true` and a `maxItems` extends one with only `uniqueItems: true`.

### Standard Schemas are read as their JSON Schema

A Standard Schema is read as the JSON Schema of its input, so what that can't express, like Zod's refinements, transforms and `undefined`, is invisible, and `true` proves the relation only for those JSON Schemas:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"
import { z } from "zod"

const X = fromJsonSchema(z.string().refine(s => s === "x"))

// the refinement isn't in its JSON Schema
fromJsonSchema(z.string()).extends(X) // true
```

A `format` like Zod's `z.url()` writes is an annotation, as JSON Schema defaults to, so it accepts any string too.

### arktype objects can be arrays

ArkType's `object` includes arrays, like TypeScript's. JSON Schema's `"object"` excludes them. An arktype Type is compared with its own meaning, so it accepts values a JSON Schema with the same properties doesn't:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const User = type({ name: "string" })

const JsonUser = fromJsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: { name: { type: "string" } },
	required: ["name"]
})

JsonUser.extends(User) // true
// User accepts Object.assign([], { name: "" })
User.extends(JsonUser) // false
fromJsonSchema(User.toJsonSchema()).extends(JsonUser) // true
```

To compare a Type with JSON's meaning, read its `.toJsonSchema()` with `fromJsonSchema`.

### OpenAPI

OpenAPI 3.0's `nullable: true` adds `null` to the `type` beside it, as ajv reads it, and the schema's other keywords still apply, so `{ type: "string", enum: ["x"], nullable: true }` is `"x"`. A `nullable` without a `type`, like one beside a `$ref`, throws a `ParseError` naming its pointer, as ajv does. A `$ref` into a document's `components` resolves when the document is spread into the schema that refers to it, as [From JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema#how-it-reads-json-schema) shows.

## Combining

`.and()` returns a Type of the values both accept, and `.or()` one of the values either accepts, without a branch another already accepts. `.and()` throws a `ParseError` if no value satisfies both, so check `.overlaps()` first if they may not:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"
import { z } from "zod"

const User = fromJsonSchema(z.object({ id: z.string(), age: z.number() }))

const Capped = User.and(
	fromJsonSchema({ type: "object", properties: { age: { maximum: 120 } } })
)

Capped.expression // "{ age: number <= 120, id: string } & isNonArray"

fromJsonSchema(z.string()).or(fromJsonSchema({ type: "number" })).expression // "number | string"
```

## Normalizing

`.toJsonSchema()` writes any of them back as JSON Schema, so it converts a schema from any format, or normalizes one JSON Schema into another:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

fromJsonSchema({
	$defs: { Name: { type: "string" } },
	allOf: [{ $ref: "#/$defs/Name" }, { minLength: 2 }]
}).toJsonSchema()
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "string",
	"minLength": 2
}
```

It takes the [usual options](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema) and throws the same way. A keyword read opaquely, like `uniqueItems`, has no JSON Schema of its own once it's read, so handle its `predicate` [fallback](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes):

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

fromJsonSchema({ type: "array", uniqueItems: true }).toJsonSchema({
	fallback: { predicate: ctx => ({ ...ctx.base, uniqueItems: true }) }
})
```

# Keyword support

> How fromJsonSchema reads each JSON Schema keyword, which ones throw, and which are only annotations.

A Type read from a schema by [`fromJsonSchema`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema), directly or as a Standard Schema's JSON Schema, accepts exactly what a JSON Schema 2020-12 validator accepts, except that lengths count UTF-16 code units, with ajv as the tiebreaker. Each keyword is read in one of five ways:

- **supported**: the Type checks it, and [comparisons](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/compare) like `.extends()` reason about it.
- **opaque**: the Type checks it exactly, with a predicate. Comparisons through it can't be proven, and `toJsonSchema()` needs a [`predicate` fallback](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) to write it back.
- **annotation**: kept as the Type's metadata, and not validated.
- **throws**: reading the schema throws a `ParseError` naming the keyword's JSON Pointer.
- **ignored**: has no effect.

Every keyword in a schema applies, and a type's keywords constrain only that type while leaving the other JSON types unconstrained: `{ minimum: 5 }` accepts `"foo"` and other JSON values like `null` or `{}`, rejects `-1` and non-JSON values like `undefined`, `bigint`, `symbol`, or functions, and `{ type: ["string", "number"], minLength: 2 }` accepts `3` but not `"a"`.

[`configure()`](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration) doesn't change what a schema accepts: whatever `onUndeclaredKey`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `numberAllowsNaN` and `numberAllowsInfinity` say, an object allows keys it doesn't declare, an optional property can't be `undefined`, and a number is finite.

A keyword with an invalid value throws, like `#/minLength must be a non-negative integer (was -1)`. A keyword JSON Schema doesn't define is ignored.

Of OpenAPI 3.0's own forms, which `toJsonSchema({ target: "openapi-3.0" })` writes, only `nullable` is read: beside a `type`, `nullable: true` adds `null` to that type as ajv reads it, so a sibling `enum` must list `null` too; without a `type` — beside `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `$ref`, `enum`, `const`, or any other subschema — `nullable: true` unions the schema with `null`. `example` is ignored, and a boolean `exclusiveMinimum` throws.

`fromJsonSchema` checks a schema written in the call as you write it: an invalid keyword value is a type error, as is each keyword below that throws, except a `$ref` to another document. See [Invalid schemas](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema#invalid-schemas).

## Core

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `true`, `false` | supported | `unknown` and `never` |
| `type` | supported | a name or an array of names. `"object"` excludes arrays and functions |
| `const`, `enum` | supported | objects and arrays are compared by value |
| `$ref` | supported | `#`, a JSON Pointer like `#/$defs/Node`, an anchor or an embedded `$id`, including recursive refs |
| `$ref` to another document | **throws** | only refs into the same document are resolved |
| `$defs`, `definitions` | supported | read where a `$ref` points to them. Each value must be a schema |
| `$dynamicRef`, `$recursiveRef` | **throws** | ignored under a draft-07 or earlier `$schema`, which has neither |
| `title`, `description`, `default`, `examples`, `deprecated` | annotation | `default` is not applied |
| `$schema` | annotation | draft-07 or earlier ignores the keywords beside a `$ref`, as those drafts do |
| `$id`, `$anchor`, `$dynamicAnchor` | supported | identify a schema a `$ref` resolves to. Draft-04 reads `id` |
| `$comment`, `readOnly`, `writeOnly` | **ignored** | |
| `contentEncoding`, `contentMediaType` | **ignored** | annotations in 2020-12 |
| `nullable` (OpenAPI 3.0) | supported | adds `null` to the `type` beside it, or unions the schema with `null` without a `type`. **Throws** if `false` beside `"null"` |

## Composition

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `allOf`, `anyOf` | supported | |
| `oneOf` | supported | when its branches are disjoint, it's a union. Otherwise, opaque |
| `not` | opaque | |
| `if`, `then`, `else` | opaque | `if` without `then` or `else` has no effect |

Composition keywords apply together and beside any other keyword:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const T = fromJsonSchema({
	anyOf: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }],
	not: { const: 0 }
})

T.allows("a") // true
// ArkErrors: must be other than 0
T(0)
```

## Strings

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `minLength`, `maxLength` | supported | counts UTF-16 code units, as arktype's bounds do, where JSON Schema counts code points |
| `pattern` | supported | a string, or a `RegExp` read with its own flags |
| `format` | annotation | as the spec defaults to, and as `toJsonSchema()` writes it |

## Numbers

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `minimum`, `maximum` | supported | |
| `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum` | supported | a number. Draft 4's boolean form throws |
| `multipleOf` | supported | an integer. Any other positive number, opaque |

## Arrays

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `prefixItems`, `items` | supported | prefix elements are optional, as JSON Schema says: `[string?, number?, ...unknown[]]`. `items` is the rest |
| `items` as an array, `additionalItems` | supported | draft-07's tuples |
| `minItems`, `maxItems` | supported | |
| `uniqueItems` | opaque | items are compared as JSON values |
| `contains`, `minContains`, `maxContains` | opaque | `minContains: 0` without `maxContains` has no effect |
| `unevaluatedItems` | **throws** | ignored under a draft-07 or earlier `$schema`, which has no such keyword |

## Objects

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `properties`, `required` | supported | a `required` key not in `properties` must be present, with any value. See below |
| `patternProperties` | supported | |
| `additionalProperties` | supported | `false` rejects other keys. A schema is an index signature alone, or opaque beside `properties` |
| `propertyNames`, `minProperties`, `maxProperties` | opaque | one every object meets, like `propertyNames: { type: "string" }`, has no effect |
| `dependentRequired`, `dependentSchemas`, `dependencies` | opaque | one every object meets, like `dependentRequired: { a: [] }`, has no effect |
| `unevaluatedProperties` | **throws** | ignored under a draft-07 or earlier `$schema`, which has no such keyword |

A JSON object's properties are its own, so `required: ["toString"]` rejects `{}`, though `{}` inherits `toString` from `Object.prototype`. A property named by a key `Object.prototype` has is read as a pattern that matches only that key, which, unlike a property, checks an own key alone:

```ts
import { fromJsonSchema } from "arktype"

const T = fromJsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: { toString: { type: "string" } }
})

T.expression // "{ [/^toString$/]: string } & isNonArray"
T.allows({}) // true
```
